newsitem.title: USA: Shadow U.S. regulators favor bank and commerce mix.
newsitem.headline: Shadow U.S. regulators favor bank and commerce mix.

text.p: A regulatory advisory group composed of academic and private sector banking experts urged Congress on Monday to eliminate the legal barriers separating banking from commercial businesses.

"It is unwise for the government to interfere with the quest of private actors to develop organizational forms that will facilitate the most efficient allocation of resources," the Shadow Financial Regulatory Commission said in a policy statement.
The separation of banking and commerce has been one of the most controversial issues in the banking law reform debate.
Legislation introduced by Rep. Richard Baker, Republican of Louisiana, and Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato, Republican of New York, would completely eliminate the separation.
A bill sponsored by Rep Marge Roukema, Republican of New Jersey, would allow banks to conduct up to 25 percent of their business in non-financial activities.
But some lawmakers, including House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach, are opposed to any significant mixing.
The Clinton administration has yet to issue its proposal, but is said to be leaning towards allowing some mixing.
While favoring unlimited mixing subject to existing antitrust rules, the shadow regulators said both sides in the debate had offered exaggerated arguments.
The group said, for example, that banks would not be likely to bias their lending decisions to favor a commercial affiliate, as some critics have charged.

"Current law and regulation already address the potential concern about conflicts of interest by requiring all bank loans to bank affiliates or subsidiaries to be made on arms-length condistions, to be fully collateralized and to be subject to legal limits," the group said.
But proponents have also overstated their case, the group said. "It is important not to expect dramatic benefits from doing so, at least in the short run," the group said.
On a related bank reform issue, the shadow regulators urged that the debate not bog down over the issue of government's alleged subsidy to the banking industry.

Some regulators, most notably Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, argue that banks receive benefits from the government from deposit insurance and access to the payments system. They suggest that bank reform be structured to limit the subsidy from spreading to a bank's non-banking activities.
But others, including Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig, maintain that because banks must abide by numerous government regulations, there is no net benefit from the alleged subsidy.
The shadow regulators said they were skeptical any significant net subsidy existed and said the Fed could eliminate any subsidy by charging market rates for the services involved.

"If the Fed is concerned about the subsidy, they can take the action to do away with the subsidy," Emory University professor George Benston told reporters at a news briefing. "It's rather ironic that the Fed says it should have control because of a subsidy that it itself creates."
Nobel laureate economist Franco Modigliani of Columbia University said, in his personal view, no subsidy existed.
"If there were, than charters for banks would be valuable and the evidence suggests that charters have no significant benefit," Modigliani said at the briefing.
